messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 55, Yusuf, a married Middle Eastern farmer, described a life that had once been organized by the rhythm of his land: before dawn, fields, irrigation, repairs, the steady physical certainty of work. The assault that changed this began on an ordinary evening after he had been counting supplies near the edge of his property, when men he did not know approached as if they had a reason to be there. He remembered the sudden shift in their expressions, the sense of people acting suspiciously, and then the attack itself in broken shards: a hand grabbing at his shirt, the sting of impact, the smell of sweat and body odour close to his face, his own heart racing so hard that he could hear it in his ears. When he tries to tell the story now, Yusuf says the memory does not stay in one line; it comes in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, and when he attempts to explain what happened he loses the thread and cannot finish. What remains most painfully present to him is that the memory feels as though it belongs to someone else rather than to him, as if he is describing the experience of another man.

In the weeks that followed, those fragments did not settle into a coherent account; instead, they seemed to push him toward repeated attempts to make sense of what had happened and what he should do about it. Yusuf found himself ruminating on revenge, returning again and again to how he might get even with the assailant, rehearsing possibilities while he worked. The more the memory failed him—breaking apart whenever he tried to speak, refusing to become a story he could control—the more he clung to these thoughts of retaliation, as though planning retribution might give shape to something that otherwise felt unreal and humiliating. He no longer trusted the possibility of simply leaving the event behind in words, because every attempt to recount it ended in frustration and shame, and that frustration fed back into the same bitter circles of thought. He reported that he now throws himself into work and tasks to keep his mind occupied, taking on extra labor in the fields and staying busy with repairs that do not truly need doing, because unoccupied time allows the fragments to return and the revenge fantasies to gather force.

Certain moments now pull him immediately back into that state. When Yusuf notices his own heart racing or pounding—whether from exertion in the heat or from a sudden jolt of alarm—he becomes convinced that danger is near, and his mind returns to the assault with fresh urgency. A man standing too close, especially one whose sweat or body odour reaches him in the farmyard or at the market, can have the same effect; he reads the sensation as a warning and feels the old threat tightening around him. On those occasions he does not stay still to examine his fear. He turns back to work, pushes himself harder, or fills the rest of the day with tasks, partly to avoid the anniversary dates connected to the attack and partly because stillness gives his mind room to spiral toward revenge. The cycle has narrowed his life: he is more guarded around others, less able to remain present with his wife in the evenings, and more often absent from ordinary conversation because he is preoccupied with what he did not see clearly and what he might have done differently.

For Yusuf, the most frightening part is that the assault no longer feels like a finished event. The fragments remain outside his control, and the bodily signs that remind him of it make him feel as if the danger is happening again, pushing him back into work and into thoughts of getting even. He finally sought help after realizing that the dates around the assault had become impossible to face and that he was spending more and more of his days trying not to think. He hopes to sleep without being dragged back into the scattered pieces, but what he fears most is that, if he stops keeping himself busy, the memory will come apart again and the urge for revenge will take over his life.
